title: How to Choose a Cut-and-Sew POD Partner Like Apliiq
excerpt: A decision framework for DTC brands picking a cut-and-sew print-on-demand partner: what to test in samples, how to model unit costs, and when stock blanks still win.
body: Cut-and-sew is a different buying decision from standard print-on-demand. Instead of picking a blank garment and adding a print, you are choosing a partner that controls the fabric, the pattern, the trims, and the stitch quality that shows up at your customer's door. That adds design flexibility you cannot get from a shared catalog of stock blanks, and it adds risk you cannot simply return. Before you commit ad spend, run the decision through a few fixed tests rather than a gut feel about how the mockups look.

Start with the garment itself. Order samples in three sizes from the same style line and wash them five times. Look for seam twist, collar curl, shrinkage beyond five percent, and print cracking at the stress points. A partner worth building a brand on will tolerate this scrutiny and will tell you plainly which fabrics hold up and which do not. If the answer stays vague, that is the answer. Write the results into a simple scorecard so the next person on your team can repeat the test without relitigating taste every season.

Then model the unit economics honestly. Cut-and-sew carries a higher base cost, higher minimums in many cases, and longer lead times, but it can remove the price pressure you face when every competitor sells the identical blank. Build a landed cost per unit that includes fabric, cut, print, labeling, packaging, and outbound shipping to your customer. Compare that number against your target contribution margin, not against the cheapest catalog tee you can find in a marketplace search.

Lead time is the third test. Ask how long a reorder takes from purchase order to shipped parcel, and ask what happens in the fourth quarter when capacity tightens. A partner that promises seven days in February and delivers in twenty-one days in November will quietly break every launch calendar you build. Get the peak-season number in writing and plan your marketing around it rather than hoping the calendar bends for you.

Decide where cut-and-sew actually earns its keep. It usually pays for itself on hero products with a distinctive silhouette, private label basics you plan to restock for years, and bundles where the packaging matters as much as the print. It rarely pays for itself on experimental designs you intend to kill after one campaign. Keep the experimental volume on stock blanks and reserve the slower, more expensive process for the items that define the brand.

Treat the first ninety days as a pilot. Run two styles, cap the SKU count, and review return reasons weekly. Cut-and-sew quality problems surface in returns long before they show up in reviews, and a small return spike on a new pattern is cheap to fix compared with a full-season buy. Once the defect rate is flat and the reorder rhythm is predictable, widen the line.
